line_before: Ooh, can we turn this over together for a second?
line_now: Can we look at this together for a second, really gently?
why: Pipzi opener that isn't tender, so it opens any heavy feeling that isn't detected as grief. In my probe it opened 'He calls me names and puts me down every night', which passes the screen. 'Ooh' sounds delighted by distress, and 'turn this over' asks the person to re-see what is happening to them. The rewrite keeps Pipzi's together-curiosity without the relish.

line_before: Let’s float up onto a cloud and look down at this for a moment.
line_now: Let’s sit on a quiet hilltop for a moment and look at this from a little further off.
why: 'Float up and look down' is afterlife and escape imagery. 'I just want to float away from it all' passes the screen, and in my probe it got this opener. Grief that isn't detected ('since he passed') can get it too. The hilltop keeps Zuzu's outdoor whimsy and the step-back idea.

line_before: Imagine this feeling as weather, passing over a big, wide sky.
line_now: Imagine this feeling as weather, and you as the big, wide sky that can hold it.
why: This is Zuzu's only soft (tender) heavy opener, so every detected grief that gets Zuzu opens with it, stillbirth included (12 of 84 for 'We lost the baby at 12 weeks'). 'Passing' says grief will blow over, echoes 'passed away', and contradicts line 53. The rewrite still makes no assumption that the feeling is hard, so it stays soft.

line_before: Feeling {adj}? Fair enough. Let’s look at this straight.
line_now: Feeling {adj}? Fair enough. Let’s look at this straight.
why: This is Glitzi's dry voice, which is the personality the owner wants. In Australian English 'Fair enough' means acceptance, not doubt, and the line goes on to engage. It isn't tender, so it never opens detected grief. The tone is merely imperfect, so it doesn't warrant flattening Glitzi.

line_before: Ugh. That sounds rough, honestly.
line_now: Honestly? That sounds really, really hard.
why: Tagged tender, so it is one of only two Glitzi openers for detected grief (43 and 46). It opened 'We lost the baby at 12 weeks' and 'My dad is dying' 7 of 84 times each. 'Ugh... rough' is flippant for a death or a suicide loss. The rewrite keeps Glitzi's 'Honestly?' bluntness.

line_before: Missing someone this much can be a measure of how much they mattered. Grief doesn’t need to be tidied away or hurried along.
line_now: Missing someone this much can be a measure of how much they matter. Grief doesn’t need to be tidied away or hurried along.
why: Found by the Tier 0 code review. 'How much they mattered' is past tense, the flaw fixed in line 54: the loss cues include 'is dying', so 'My dad is dying' gets this line while he is still alive. 'Matter' fits a death that hasn't happened yet as well as one that has, and a pregnancy loss.

line_before: Maybe there’s a small way to keep them close today: a song, a place, or a story you could share with someone who’d love to hear it.
line_now: If it feels right, there might be a small way to mark this today: a quiet moment, a song, or a few words with someone who gets it.
why: Loss cues include miscarriage and 'is dying', and any death, including an abusive parent's. 'Keep them close' and a story 'someone would love to hear' assume a loving bond and shared memories, which can sting. The rewrite keeps the connection kind and leaves room for private or mixed grief.

line_before: There’s no right amount of time for this. Still feeling it, weeks or years on, can simply be what love looks like later.
line_now: There’s no right amount of time for this, and no right way to feel it. However long the feeling stays, it can simply be what love looks like.
why: Found by the Tier 0 code review. 'Weeks or years on' and 'later' assume the death has already happened, so they're wrong for 'My dad is dying', the flaw fixed in line 54. The rewrite keeps 'no right amount of time' and 'what love looks like', and fits before and after a death. 'However long the feeling stays' (not 'it lasts') so it can't be read as how long the person has left.

line_before: You don’t have to carry this on your own. Talking to someone who knew them, or someone who simply listens well, might help a little.
line_now: You don’t have to carry this on your own. Talking with someone who understands, or someone who simply listens well, might help a little.
why: 'Knew them' is past tense. Confirmed in my probes: it reaches 'My dad is dying' (11 of 84), where the person is still alive, and 'We lost the baby' (10 of 84), where often nobody else knew the baby. The rewrite keeps the help-seeking message and fits every loss cue.

line_before: Could a small thread of contact help, like a message, a voice note or a photo, even if it can’t close the distance?
line_now: Could a small thread of connection help, like an old photo, a familiar song, or a chat with someone who gets it, even if it can’t close the distance?
why: Confirmed: 'I miss him so much since he passed' isn't detected as grief and got this line 32 of 84 times (loneliness), which means suggesting a message to someone who has died. 'I miss my ex so much even though he hurt me' got it 13 of 84 times. The rewrite moves contact away from the missed person and works for death, an ex or distance.

line_before: A silence between people who were close isn’t always the end of the story. Sometimes it’s a long pause that neither person knows how to break first.
line_now: A silence between people who were close can hold a lot: hurt, missing, even relief. It doesn’t have to be solved today, and what it means can get clearer with time.
why: Confirmed as the top line (29 of 84) for 'Dad cut me off when I came out'. It guesses that the other person wants to reconnect and presses toward contact, including for someone who cut off an abuser for safety. The rewrite keeps the time kind and allows distance.

line_before: Nobody can see how the future goes, for anyone. What you can choose is how you spend the time that’s here.
line_now: Nobody can see exactly how things will go. If something about them is worrying you, it’s okay to check in with them, and to lean on someone for support too.
why: Confirmed 38 of 84 for 'worried about my brother, he's drinking every night and talking about being a burden', which passes the screen. 'The time that's here' sounds like the time is running out, and the line steers toward acceptance when checking in and getting support are the right moves.

line_before: Being worn out can make everything feel heavier and more final than it is. Some of this might look different after proper rest.
line_now: Being worn out can make everything feel heavier and harder to hold. It’s okay to go easy on yourself, and on big conclusions, while you’re this tired.
why: The tired theme isn't notWithGrief. 'Mum passed away last month and I'm exhausted' got this line 19 of 84 times, beside the loss lines, telling a bereaved person it is 'more final than it is' and that rest may change it. The rewrite drops the false claim and keeps the protective 'go easy on big conclusions'.

line_before: Could one small kindness for your body help a little today: water, food, fresh air, or an earlier night?
line_now: Could one small kindness for your body help a little today: water, a warm drink, some fresh air, or a rest?
why: This theme's own cues include 'can't sleep' and 'not sleeping', so 'an earlier night' misses the point, and 'food' can be fraught. A small wording change fixes a mismatch that comes from the theme's own cues.

line_before: Feeling torn often means both options hold something you care about. That’s less like being stuck and more like having two good reasons.
line_now: Feeling torn can mean a lot is riding on this, and that’s heavy to hold on your own. It’s okay not to have the answer yet.
why: Confirmed: 'I'm not sure if I can keep going like this' (worry) passes the screen and got this line 44 of 84 times. 'Should I leave him or stay? He's so controlling' got it 47 of 84 times. Calling both paths 'good reasons' endorses not going on, or staying with a controlling partner. The rewrite endorses neither and hints at sharing the load.

line_before: Imagine yourself a year from now, having chosen each path in turn. Which version of you seems to breathe out a little?
line_now: Imagine someone kind, who knows you well, hearing all of this. What might they say matters most to you here?
why: The top line (35 of 84) for 'I'm not sure if I can keep going like this' with no label or confusion. Picturing each path and choosing the one that brings relief is exactly what safe-messaging warns against when one hidden path is not being here. The rewrite keeps the other-eyes kind.

line_before: There may not be a perfect option, only real ones with different trade-offs. Choosing one you can live with is allowed.
line_now: There may not be a perfect option here. It’s okay to take your time, and to talk it through with someone you trust before you choose.
why: Reaches the same veiled-ideation and controlling-partner texts (up to 15 of 84), where 'choosing one you can live with is allowed' reads as permission. The rewrite adds time and talking it through.

line_before: From the outside, other people’s friendships can look finished and easy. Lots of them were built slowly, through small repeated moments.
line_now: From the outside, other people’s friendships can look ready-made and easy. Lots of them were built slowly, through small repeated moments.
why: 'Finished' reads as 'ended', which confuses a lonely reader. A one-word change, same voice.

line_before: Some of the people around you might feel more on the edge than they show. Loneliness tends to be quieter than it is rare.
line_now: Some of the people around you might feel more on the outside than they show. Loneliness is often more common than it looks, just quieter.
why: 'On the edge' usually means near breaking point, and 'quieter than it is rare' is hard to parse. The meaning was 'on the outside, and common'.

line_before: Your frustration might be pointing at something real: the load doesn’t feel shared. That’s worth saying out loud, kindly and plainly.
line_now: This feeling might be pointing at something real: the load doesn’t feel shared. If it feels safe to, that’s worth saying out loud, kindly and plainly.
why: Confirmed 29 to 33 of 84 for 'My husband never helps with the kids and gets nasty if I bring it up', which neither NOT_CHORES nor the screen catches, so it nudges toward confronting a volatile partner. It also tells a sad or angry person they feel 'frustration'. The rewrite adds a safety condition and stops naming the feeling for them.

line_before: Could there be one specific ask, like a rota or a single job that’s theirs, rather than a general plea for help?
line_now: If it feels okay to ask, could there be one specific thing, like a roster or a single job that’s theirs, rather than a general plea for help?
why: 'Rota' is British; Australians say 'roster'. It got 25 of 84 for the 'gets nasty if I bring it up' text, so it needs the same safety condition as 79.

line_before: Waiting for health news, yours or someone else’s, can send the mind racing ahead. Not knowing yet is hard, and it isn’t the same as bad news.
line_now: Health worries, yours or someone else’s, can send the mind racing ahead. Whatever you know so far, it’s okay to take this one small step at a time.
why: Health cues include diagnos*, scan and hospital, so the line reaches people who already have bad news. 'The scan showed there's no heartbeat' got it 13 of 84 times: 'it isn't the same as bad news' is false and cruel there. The rewrite fits before and after news.

line_before: It might help to jot down your questions before the appointment, so some of this has somewhere to go.
line_now: If there’s an appointment coming up, it might help to jot down your questions first, so some of this has somewhere to go.
why: It assumes an appointment exists. The health theme also fires beside a death in hospital, since it isn't notWithGrief. Making the appointment conditional keeps the practical help where it fits, such as the top pick (35 of 84) after a cancer diagnosis.

line_before: You don’t have to hold the waiting on your own. Telling one person you trust could make it a little lighter.
line_now: You don’t have to hold this on your own. Telling one person you trust could make it a little lighter.
why: 'The waiting' assumes there is no news yet, which doesn't fit after a diagnosis. Dropping one word makes it fit every health context.

line_before: Nerves before a test can be a sign you care how it goes, rather than a forecast of how it will go.
line_now: Nerves before a test can be a sign you care how it goes, rather than a forecast of how it will go.
why: The line is kind and right for exams, and not unkind before a medical test either: nerves aren't a forecast. The misfire after 'another negative test today' comes from the exam cue catching medical and pregnancy tests and from notWhen lacking 'negative'. No rewording can fix that. The owner should fix the cue, not the line. Done in the Tier 0 code review: the exam theme steps aside when health or pregnancy words appear anywhere in the words (MEDICAL_WORDS), 'negative test' included.

line_before: One exam measures one day’s work on one set of questions. It isn’t a measure of you, or of everything you’ll do next.
line_now: One exam measures one day’s work on one set of questions. It isn’t a measure of you, or of everything you’ll do next.
why: Confirmed 54 of 84 for 'I have a test on Thursday to see if the cancer is back'. That is a real 'the Mallow didn't listen' moment, but the line says nothing hurtful, and any exam line would mismatch there. Keep it, and stop the exam cue (tests? on/today/tomorrow) matching medical, blood, pregnancy or cancer tests. Done in the Tier 0 code review: the exam theme steps aside when health or pregnancy words appear anywhere in the words (MEDICAL_WORDS), so 'a test on Thursday to see if the cancer is back' gets health lines only.

line_before: Studying while stressed is harder than it looks from the outside. Doing some of it, imperfectly, still counts.
line_now: Getting work done while stressed is harder than it looks from the outside. Doing some of it, imperfectly, still counts.
why: The study cue includes 'deadlines', so work stress gets a line about studying. The rewrite covers both, same voice.

line_before: Being stuck is often part of getting better, even when it doesn’t feel like progress. The awkward middle bit counts.
line_now: Feeling stuck after trying this hard is exhausting, and it isn’t a sign you’ve failed. Some things need more than effort alone, and that’s okay.
why: The 'trying' cue fires on any 'trying/tried'. Confirmed as the top line (47 of 84) for 'I tried to leave him last month but he would not let me', which passes the screen, and 19 of 84 for daily chronic pain. 'Part of getting better' frames being trapped as progress and promises recovery. The rewrite holds up for leaving an abuser, chronic pain, infertility and learning a skill.

line_before: Could you make the next try smaller, or ask someone for a fresh pair of eyes? Sometimes that’s all it takes to get unstuck.
line_now: Could someone you trust look at this with you, or help you think through the next step? You don’t have to get unstuck alone.
why: The top line (42 of 84) for 'I keep trying to get better but the pain is still bad every single day', and 14 of 84 for the 'he would not let me leave' text. 'That's all it takes' trivialises, and 'make the next try smaller' is unsafe advice about leaving a controlling partner. The rewrite keeps the agency kind and points to support.

line_before: A no from one place is a decision about one application at one moment. It isn’t a verdict on what you’re capable of.
line_now: A no from one place is a decision about one application at one moment. It isn’t a verdict on you.
why: 'Unsuccessful' catches IVF (32 of 84 for 'Our IVF round was unsuccessful again') and disability-support refusals. There, 'what you're capable of' lands on the body or reads as an assessment of capacity. A shorter ending removes the sting and still works for jobs.

line_before: Disappointment this sharp often means you let yourself hope, and hoping took courage.
line_now: A hurt this sharp often means you let yourself hope, and hoping took courage.
why: The rejection theme isn't notWithGrief, so 'The operation was unsuccessful and dad died' can pair a death with 'disappointment'. Changing one word makes it right for a death, IVF (its top context, 39 of 84) and a job alike.

line_before: Nerves and excitement can feel almost the same in the body. Some of this might be your body getting ready.
line_now: Nerves before a big moment are very normal. They can feel loud in the body without meaning it will go badly.
why: Confirmed 32 of 84 for 'I have a police interview tomorrow about what he did to me', and 14 of 84 beside the loss lines for 'First day back at work tomorrow after the miscarriage'. 'Your body getting ready' is cruel after a pregnancy loss, and 'excitement' jars. The rewrite also removes the duplicate of line 157's opening sentence.

line_before: Money worries tend to feel bigger in the fog. Writing down what’s due and when might shrink it to something you can plan around.
line_now: Money worries can feel even heavier in a fog. Writing down what’s due and when might make the next step a little easier to see.
why: The top line (32 of 84) for 'I cannot afford food for the kids this week and the rent is already overdue'. 'Feel bigger' and 'shrink it' imply real hardship is partly perception. The rewrite keeps the practical step without that suggestion.

line_before: Being stretched for money is stressful, and it says nothing about your worth. A lot of it comes down to things outside your control.
line_now: Being stretched for money is stressful, and it says nothing about your worth. It happens to all sorts of people, for all sorts of reasons.
why: The top line (37 of 84) for 'I lost my rent money on the pokies again'. Stating the cause as outside the person's control is a claim the Mallow can't make, and it brushes past gambling harm. The worth message, which matters for shame, is kept.

line_before: If it keeps feeling tight, a free money advice service could help you sort out the next steps, without judgement.
line_now: If money keeps feeling tight, or scary, a free financial counsellor could help you sort out the next steps, without judgement.
why: This is the money theme's only signpost, and 'money advice service' is a UK term. In Australia the free help is financial counselling. 'Tight' alone also understates real hardship.

line_before: It doesn’t all need planning yet. The looking-forward part is part of the good bit too.
line_now: The looking-forward part is part of the good bit too. Plan whatever helps you feel ready, and let the rest wait.
why: 'Moving out next week to get away from him. Finally!' (excitement) got this line 19 of 84 times. 'It doesn't all need planning yet' is wrong at a high-risk point in a separation. The rewrite keeps the savouring and stops discouraging planning.

line_before: Worry tends to speak in what-ifs. It can feel like a warning, even when it’s really a guess about something that hasn’t happened.
line_now: Worry tends to speak in what-ifs. Some are guesses, and some are worth listening to, especially when they’re about your safety.
why: label:worry is the fallback for fears no theme matches. Confirmed 21 of 84 for 'I am scared he will turn up at my work again', 17 of 84 for 'I am scared of what he will do when he gets home tonight' and 19 of 84 for 'My son hasn't come home'. All pass the screen. Calling a safety fear 'really a guess' contradicts the app's own copy telling people to trust that feeling.

line_before: Maybe split this into two piles: the parts you can do something about, and the parts that can only be waited out.
line_now: Maybe split this into two piles: the parts you can do something about, and the parts you might want some help with.
why: The top line (30 of 84) for 'I am scared of what he will do when he gets home tonight', and 19 of 84 for a missing son. 'Can only be waited out' nudges toward doing nothing when someone may be in danger. The rewrite keeps the agency kind and points to help.

line_before: Think of a past worry that felt this big. How did that one turn out, and what helped you through it?
line_now: Think of another time something felt this big. What helped you get through it, even a little?
why: The top line (30 of 84) for 'He always hurts me when he drinks', which passes the screen. 'How did that one turn out' assumes past fears came to nothing, and for this person they came true. The rewrite keeps the resource question without assuming the outcome.

line_before: Feeling low can make the whole picture look grey, even the parts that aren’t. It might be worth going easy on big conclusions today.
line_now: Feeling this low can make everything look grey at once. It might help to go gently today, and leave big decisions for later.
why: The top line (23 of 84) for 'We lost our little one at twelve weeks', a pregnancy loss the loss cues miss. 'Even the parts that aren't' frames grief as distorted thinking. The delay message protects anyone with ideation that slipped past the screen, so it is kept.

line_before: What would a fair outcome look like here? Knowing that can turn the heat into a clear, calm ask.
line_now: What would a fair outcome look like here? Knowing that can help you work out what you need next.
why: The top line (31 of 84) for 'My ex turned up drunk last night and screamed at me in front of the kids', and 21 of 84 for 'Someone touched me at the party'. Both pass the screen. A 'calm ask' of the person who did the harm is unsafe and puts the burden on the person who was hurt.

line_before: Anger often makes its point best once it has cooled a little. Waiting before you reply might help it land the way you mean it.
line_now: Anger often gets clearer once it has cooled a little. You don’t owe anyone a quick reply, and there’s no rush to decide what to do with it.
why: In the abuse and assault contexts that reach label:anger, it polices the person's tone and assumes they will reply to whoever hurt them. The rewrite keeps the 'let it cool' idea as permission, not coaching.

line_before: You might not have the whole story yet about why it happened. That doesn’t make it okay, but it might change what you do next.
line_now: You don’t need the whole story of why it happened for your anger to count. It’s okay to start with what you need.
why: Confirmed 19 of 84 for the screamed-at-in-front-of-the-kids text, and it also came up for the party assault. It invites the person to look for the harmer's reasons, close to victim-blaming. The rewrite keeps 'you don't know why' but makes the anger valid without it.

line_before: Could you reach out to one person, even in a small way? A short message can open a door without asking much of anyone.
line_now: Could you reach out to one person, in a small way that feels safe? A quick hello can open a door without asking much of anyone.
why: 'He checks my phone so I cannot really message anyone' got this line 12 of 84 times. Under coercive control, prompting a message can be unsafe. Adding 'feels safe' and saying 'hello' instead of 'message' fixes it while keeping the connection nudge for everyone else.

line_before: If someone who cares about you saw this, what might they notice that’s harder to see from the inside?
line_now: If someone kind were reading this with you, what might they notice that’s harder to see from the inside?
why: 'Nobody cares whether I am here or not' passes the screen with no label and got this line 19 of 84 times. Assuming someone cares contradicts what the person just said, at a moment close to passive ideation.

line_before: Lots of people read a message, mean to reply later, and then life swallows it. The reply they wrote in their head can feel like a sent one.
why: unanswered-message. The top line (35 of 84) for a friend's 'thanks for everything' message followed by silence (a warning sign that passes the screen), 12 of 84 for a low daughter silent for three days, and 14 of 84 for a bereaved person texting a dead father's phone. Explaining the silence away can delay a welfare check, which Reframe's own safety note says to make first.

line_before: They might be waiting until they have the time or energy to reply properly, rather than firing off something quick.
why: unanswered-message, benign kind. It gives a kind excuse for a silence that may be a welfare emergency, or a partner's punishing silent treatment. It came up less often (3 of 84), but the excuse works against checking in.

line_before: Silence is an absence of information. It could mean almost anything — including nothing at all.
why: unanswered-message. 'Including nothing at all' brushes off a silence from someone who is low, elderly and alone, or who has just said goodbye. Its tone is also colder than any Mallow.

line_before: Maybe something is a bit off between you. If so, the silence is a clue worth checking gently, not a verdict to accept on your own.
line_now: Maybe something is a bit off between you. If so, the silence is a clue worth checking gently, not a verdict to accept on your own.
why: The one unanswered-message line that points toward checking in, which is the right move for a welfare worry. It is rare in the grief and silent-treatment contexts (2 to 6 of 84). The grief mismatch should be fixed by crowding unanswered-message when grief is detected.

line_before: Right now you have one data point: no reply yet. That’s not enough to know why.
why: unanswered-message. The top line (35 of 84) for 'My daughter hasnt replied in three days. She has been really low and I am scared something has happened.' Calling three days of silence from a low person 'one data point' frames a welfare concern as jumping to conclusions.

line_before: Wanting to hear back from someone you care about isn’t needy. It means they matter to you.
line_now: Wanting to hear back from someone you care about isn’t needy. It means they matter to you.
why: It validates the writer and excuses nobody. For the bereaved it reads as tender, if imperfect ('they matter to you'), and for a welfare worry it supports caring. 'Hear back' stings after a death, but that is grief routing: crowd unanswered-message on grief.

line_before: This is a chance to practise sitting with a little uncertainty without filling it with the scariest story.
why: unanswered-message. Both reviewers chose remove. It is therapy homework that tells a person worried about someone at risk not to imagine the worst. It came up 13 of 84 times for the 'thanks for everything' friend and 9 of 84 for the low daughter.

line_before: Managers often spot problems faster than they spot what’s working. Finding the gaps is part of their job, so criticism tends to be the loudest thing they say.
why: work-criticism. Confirmed 22 of 84 for 'My manager screams at me in front of the team and calls me useless every day', and 15 of 84 for a husband's put-downs. Calling bullying 'part of their job' misleads about a workplace harm and can keep someone enduring it. Reframe's own note says this isn't feedback to reframe.

line_before: They might be pointing out fixes because they think the work is worth getting right.
why: work-criticism, benign kind. It gives a kind motive to screaming, insults and a husband's 'useless and so am I' (10 of 84). Excusing the harmer is the clearest way these lines hurt.

line_before: Maybe this piece did miss the mark. That would mean there’s a skill to build here — not that you’re terrible at your job.
line_now: Maybe this piece did miss the mark. That would mean there’s a skill to build here — not that you’re terrible at your job.
why: It is hedged, and its main message ('not that you're terrible at your job') pushes back against a self-worth attack rather than excusing the boss. Fine for ordinary feedback. The bullying reach should be handled by crowding work-criticism when shouting, insult or harassment words appear.

line_before: Specific notes are a free map of what they care about. Next time, you’ll know where they look first.
line_now: Specific notes are a free map of what they care about. Next time, you’ll know where they look first.
why: In the screaming-boss context it is a visible mismatch (there are no 'notes'), not an excuse of anyone's motive. It is uncommon there (4 to 13 of 84) and a good line for ordinary feedback.

line_before: Guest lists often get decided by space, cost, a partner’s friends, or whoever happened to be in the chat that day — not by a ranking of people.
line_now: Guest lists often get decided by space, cost, a partner’s friends, or whoever happened to be in the chat that day — not by a ranking of people.
why: A good line for the very common party-exclusion case. It does explain away exclusion 'because of my wheelchair' (26 of 84, loneliness) and is rare beside a funeral (3 of 84). That is invalidation, not a safety risk. Crowd left-out on grief and on 'because of my [disability, race, sexuality]' words. Grief now crowds out left-out (Tier 0 code review); the disability words don't yet.

line_before: It could be that you’re not as close to this group as you’d like right now. If so, that’s real and worth noticing — and it’s something you can do something about.
line_now: It could be that you’re not as close to this group as you’d like right now. If so, that’s real and worth noticing — and it’s something you can do something about.
why: Hedged, and it validates ('that's real'). The promise of control is mild, and the phrasing is clumsy rather than harmful.

line_before: They might be tired, stressed, or distracted by something they haven’t mentioned yet.
line_now: They might be tired, stressed, or distracted by something they haven’t mentioned yet.
why: partner-distant, which HARM_AT_HOME already crowds out. The excuse reaches coercive silent treatment only rarely (2 of 84), because 'silent treatment whenever I see my friends' is missing from HARM_AT_HOME. Fix the list rather than the line.

line_before: There could be something between you that needs talking about. If so, noticing it now is a good thing, not a sign of doom.
line_now: There could be something between you that needs talking about. If so, noticing it now is a good thing, not a sign of doom.
why: Hedged, and a good line for a distant partner. 'Not a sign of doom' is dismissive for 'My wife is really sick and I'm so scared of losing her' (25 of 84), but that is the over-broad partner-distant match on any 'my wife'. It invalidates rather than endangers.

line_before: When you love someone, any change can feel loud. Your radar is working — it just can’t read the label.
line_now: When you love someone, any change can feel loud. Your radar is working — it just can’t read the label.
why: 'Your radar is working' validates, even in the silent-treatment case where it is the top line (64 of 84). It mismatches a known cancer diagnosis but isn't hurtful.

line_before: This could be a chance to practise asking directly and kindly, which tends to make relationships sturdier.
why: partner-distant. The top line (40 of 84) for 'My girlfriend broke up with me yesterday', where it implies the relationship can be fixed, and 15 of 84 for 'always on edge around him', where it nudges a frightened person to confront their partner. It also promises an outcome.

line_before: People tend to overestimate how much others notice their slip-ups. Everyone else is mostly busy with their own day.
why: mistake-judged matches any 'mistake/forgot'. Confirmed 26 of 84 for 'a patient got hurt because of me' and 21 of 84 for 'my dog... was hit by a car. It's my fault.' Calling that a 'slip-up' nobody noticed misses why the person is distressed. It also states others' minds as fact, which is why the owner already skips the similar aw-ang1.

line_before: Anyone who did notice might have thought “oops, been there” and moved on.
why: mistake-judged. 'Oops, been there' is flippant when a mistake hurt a patient or a child, and those texts get it (7 of 84).

line_before: A few people might well have noticed and been briefly annoyed. That can be true and still be a small, recoverable thing.
why: mistake-judged. 'A small, recoverable thing' is false and painful after a pet's death or a patient's injury: 22 of 84 for the dog hit by a car (worry), 17 of 84 for the patient. It breaks the library's own rule against insisting things will be fine.

line_before: You’d forgive a friend for this in about four seconds. You’re allowed the same deal.
why: mistake-judged. The top line for 'I forgot to pick up my son from school and he was missing for an hour' (29 of 84) and for the dog killed through an open gate (26 of 84). 'About four seconds' trivialises acute guilt. It is charming for small slips, but its worst context is common and hurtful. Hushmates could author its own gentler self-compassion line for mistakes.

line_before: Without their reasons, your brain is filling the gap with its harshest guess.
line_now: Without their reasons, your brain is filling the gap with its harshest guess.
why: job-rejection context. Stating what the reader's mind is doing is a mild overclaim, merely imperfect, with no harmful worst context.

line_before: Every interview is practice. You’ll walk into the next one already knowing some of the questions.
line_now: Every interview is practice. You’ll walk into the next one already knowing some of the questions.
why: A light, apt encouragement after a job rejection. The certainty is mild and the scenario fits the words.

line_before: This is a chance to say what you’d like — more notice, or a rebooked date — instead of quietly stewing.
line_now: This is a chance to say what you’d like — more notice, or a rebooked date — instead of quietly stewing.
why: 'Quietly stewing' is a little judgemental but apt for cancelled plans, and asking for a rebooked date is even reasonable for a cancelled surgery. Merely imperfect.

line_before: This might have shown you something you really want. That’s worth knowing — as a direction, not a scorecard.
line_now: This might have shown you something you really want. That’s worth knowing — as a direction, not a scorecard.
why: Uncommon in infertility contexts in my probes (the loss and trying lines dominated), hedged, and good for ordinary comparison. Crowd social-comparison on pregnancy, IVF or grief words.

line_before: Envy can work like a compass. What exactly do you want more of — and what’s one tiny step toward it?
line_now: Envy can work like a compass. What exactly do you want more of — and what’s one tiny step toward it?
why: The 'tiny step' jars when the wish is a baby after loss, but that pairing is rare (4 of 126 in the reviewer's run) and the line is a good growth angle for ordinary comparison. The fix is crowding social-comparison on pregnancy, IVF and grief words.

line_before: Family arguments often run on old scripts. The same few topics can set things off long after the original reason has gone.
why: family-argument, never crowded by HARM_AT_HOME. Confirmed as the top line (34 of 84) for 'Mum and dad had a huge fight again and dad threw a plate at her', 21 of 84 for 'My dad hits mum when he's drunk' and 27 of 84 for 'mum keeps shouting at me and my brother every night'. All pass the screen. 'Old scripts' makes violence mutual. Reframe's own note says don't reframe this.

line_before: They might be feeling just as rattled, and unsure how to come back from it.
why: family-argument. Asks someone in a violent home to empathise with the aggressor and frames the harm as a shared upset. It came up less often (3 to 6 of 84), but excusing the harmer is the most damaging message in that context.

line_before: An argument is a moment of disagreement, not the final score on a relationship.
why: family-argument. The top line (23 of 84) for 'My dad hits mum when he's drunk and they had a huge fight last night'. Calling family violence 'a moment of disagreement' minimises it and nudges toward the relationship carrying on.

line_before: You know how it ended. You don’t yet know how it’ll look once things have cooled.
why: family-argument. 25 of 84 for the plate-throwing text. In family violence, waiting for things to cool echoes the cycle and steers away from acting or getting support.

line_before: Noticing what set it off gives you choices next time: step in, step back, or change the subject.
why: family-argument. 11 of 84 for 'dad hits mum'. It makes the writer responsible for managing the aggressor's triggers, and 'step in' can read as stepping between a violent parent and the person being hurt.

line_before: They might have been annoyed with you. That happens in every relationship, and it’s usually fixable with a quick, honest chat.
why: seemed-annoyed. 12 to 16 of 84 for 'My dad snapped at me again... I never know what mood he will be in', which passes the screen and misses HARM_AT_HOME. It normalises walking on eggshells ('every relationship'), promises an outcome, and urges approaching a volatile person.

line_before: This is a chance to practise checking in instead of guessing.
line_now: This is a chance to practise checking in instead of guessing.
why: A mild approach nudge without the normalising or the promise that sank 236. For ordinary 'did they seem annoyed?' worries, checking in is good advice. Its volatile-parent reach should be handled by crowding seemed-annoyed on mood-volatility words. Done in the Tier 0 code review: mood-volatility words ('never know what mood', 'snapped at me again', 'on edge around him', 'mood swings') now crowd out seemed-annoyed, so this line no longer reaches the volatile parent.

line_before: Being tuned in to other people’s moods is a strength. It just needs a fact-check now and then.
why: seemed-annoyed. The top line (52 of 84, sadness) for the volatile-dad text. For someone watching a volatile parent, that watchfulness is a safety response, and 'it just needs a fact-check' says their read of danger is unreliable.

line_before: It might mean you need a different way of revising, or some extra help. That’s a fixable problem, not a verdict on you.
line_now: It might mean you need a different way of revising, or some extra help. That’s a fixable problem, not a verdict on you.
why: Hedged ('It might mean') and apt for grades. It reaches failed IVF only rarely (2 of 84). Crowd bad-grade on medical and pregnancy words. Done in the Tier 0 code review: health and pregnancy words (MEDICAL_WORDS) crowd out bad-grade.

line_before: You don’t yet know how much this counts, or what your options are. Find that out before deciding it’s a disaster.
why: bad-grade. The top line (24 of 84) for 'The pregnancy test was negative again, another failed round of IVF results'. 'Find that out before deciding it's a disaster' is bossy even for an exam, and hurtful there.

line_before: A result like this can show exactly where to focus. That’s more useful than a lucky pass.
line_now: A result like this can show exactly where to focus. That’s more useful than a lucky pass.
why: A mild silver lining that fits its exam context. It isn't hurtful in the contexts that reach it (8 or 9 of 84 for a failed resit).

line_before: Early dating comes with lots of uncertainty, and people have wildly different texting habits.
why: no-text-back fires on any 'stopped texting back'. The top line (29 of 84) for 'My friend said she can't do this anymore and stopped texting back', which passes the screen, and 9 to 14 of 84 for 'Mum has been so low lately and she stopped replying'. Normalising that silence can delay checking on someone at risk.

line_before: They might be busy, nervous, or not sure what to say next.
why: no-text-back, benign kind. It excuses the silence that follows warning words. Less frequent (up to 6 of 84), but in the same welfare contexts as 254.

line_before: You know they haven’t replied. You don’t know why yet, and you might never fully know.
why: no-text-back. The top line (32 of 84) for 'My daughter stopped replying to messages three days ago and nobody knows where she is'. 'You might never fully know' is frightening and fatalistic for a missing person.

line_before: This is good practice in staying steady while things are uncertain — a very useful dating skill.
why: no-text-back. 15 of 84 for the missing daughter, where it turns fear for someone's safety into a dating lesson. Even for real ghosting it frames the hurt as training.

line_before: They might be clumsy with worry. Sometimes “Why haven’t you…?” is a nervous way of saying “I want things to go well for you.”
why: family-criticism. It reached 'My dad calls me useless and stupid every day' (6 of 84, no label), which passes the screen. Recasting daily name-calling as hidden love is the classic way abuse gets minimised, against Reframe's own note on cruel criticism.

line_before: They might genuinely disapprove of this choice. You can hear that and still decide it’s your life to steer.
line_now: They might genuinely disapprove of this choice. You can hear that and still decide it’s your life to steer.
why: It assumes a 'choice', but its message ('it's your life to steer') is protective even for harsh family criticism. Merely imperfect.

line_before: You heard the words. You don’t know exactly what was behind them unless they tell you.
line_now: You heard the words. You don’t know exactly what was behind them unless they tell you.
why: Borderline. For constant name-calling it casts doubt on the meaning (7 to 9 of 84), but it neither excuses the speaker nor blames the writer, and for ordinary family criticism it is useful. Crowd family-criticism when HARM_AT_HOME matches (it already detects 'calls me useless').

line_before: This is a chance to practise holding your own view, even when someone you love disagrees.
line_now: This is a chance to practise holding your own view, even when someone you love disagrees.
why: 'Disagrees' understates verbal abuse, but the core message (hold your own view of yourself) counters internalising 'useless'. Kept for breadth, with the same family-criticism crowding fix.

line_before: A money setback is a numbers problem. Numbers can be planned around, even when it’s hard.
why: money-setback. Confirmed 21 of 84 for 'I cannot afford food for the kids this week and the rent is already overdue', and 19 of 84 for 'I am going to be homeless'. Reducing food insecurity to a 'numbers problem' that can be planned around is dismissive and misleading, and money crisis is a known risk factor.

line_before: Until the numbers are laid out, your brain fills the gaps with worst cases.
line_now: Until the numbers are laid out, your brain fills the gaps with worst cases.
why: It suggests some catastrophising, but its advice (lay the numbers out) is practical, and in the homeless context it sits beside 270 and 273, which name real hardship. Mild.

line_before: Getting through this could leave you with a clearer budget and more confidence for the next surprise.
why: money-setback. A silver lining for hardship that hints at poor budgeting. Silver linings for a hurt are already one of the owner's own reasons for skipping Reframe lines. Rare in real contexts, so the loss is small.

line_before: They might have been clumsy, thinking out loud, or trying to make conversation.
why: appearance-comment, benign kind. 10 of 84 for 'My husband calls me fat and ugly and makes comments about my body in front of his friends', which passes the screen. HARM_AT_HOME detects 'calls me fat' but doesn't crowd this scenario. Excusing repeated degradation, and body-shaming with signs of restricted eating, is harmful.

line_before: You heard one comment. You don’t know what anyone else thought, or whether they noticed at all.
line_now: You heard one comment. You don’t know what anyone else thought, or whether they noticed at all.
why: It understates repeated humiliation ('one comment'), but it is a visible mismatch rather than an excuse or blame, and for a single remark it is a good line. Fix by crowding appearance-comment when HARM_AT_HOME matches.

line_before: This could be a chance to practise a calm reply, or to notice whose voices you let decide how you feel about your body.
line_now: This could be a chance to practise a calm reply, or to notice whose voices you let decide how you feel about your body.
why: 'Whose voices you let decide' leans toward self-responsibility, but the core message (others' comments don't get to decide how you feel about your body) protects against body-image harm. Eating cues such as 'stopped eating' should route to support, which is a screen or routing question for Tier A.

line_before: Brains are built to scan for danger, so they often treat “possible” as “probable”. That’s a protective habit, not a forecast.
why: future-worry matches any 'scared/afraid/what if'. Confirmed 21 of 84 for 'What if he hurts me again?' and 10 of 84 for 'I am scared he will hurt me', both passing the screen. Telling someone their alarm about violence is 'a habit, not a forecast' contradicts the app's own copy telling people to trust that feeling.

line_before: It might go better than expected, or turn out more manageable than it looks from here.
why: future-worry. False hope when the fear is a partner's violence (up to 11 of 84) or a parent's coming death. Hedged, but it steers away from safety planning.

line_before: Right now this is a possibility, not an event. It hasn’t happened.
why: future-worry. The top line (24 of 84) for 'What if he hurts me again?', where it has happened before, and 16 to 21 of 84 for palliative care and chemo fears. It states as fact something a Mallow can't know.

line_before: Something might go wrong — and that’s fair to plan for. Preparing for a bump is different from bracing for a crash.
why: future-worry. The top line for 'I am scared he will hurt me' (34 of 84) and 'What if the chemo doesn't work?' (23 of 84). Calling assault or treatment failure 'a bump' minimises it. Line 286 keeps the useful planning idea.

line_before: The future really is unknown. That cuts both ways: it isn’t certain to go badly either.
why: future-worry. The top line (22 of 84) for 'Mum is in palliative care now... what if tonight is the last night?', and 17 to 20 of 84 for violence and chemo fears. 'It isn't certain to go badly' is false comfort beside a dying parent.

line_before: It might have been the wrong call. You can own that and learn from it without punishing yourself forever.
why: past-regret. The top line (26 of 84) for 'I regret not calling the ambulance sooner. He's gone now.' The loss cues miss 'he's gone now', and the line confirms guilt after a death, a risk Reframe's own note on this scenario names. It also passes judgement on regrets such as an abortion.

line_before: Someone might even have found it funny, or relatable.
why: awkward-moment matches on 'party' or 'replaying' alone. 9 of 84 for 'I keep replaying what happened at the party that night. I froze and could not say anything', which may describe an assault. Suggesting it was funny is cruel there.

line_before: This is a chance to practise letting a moment stay small instead of replaying it on a loop.
why: awkward-moment. 12 of 84 for the party-freeze text, and 7 of 84 for 'I keep replaying the moment the nurse told us'. It asks someone with an intrusive memory of trauma or bad news to shrink it, not seek support.

line_before: Joining in means sometimes things come out wrong. That’s the price of taking part, and it’s worth paying.
why: awkward-moment. The top line for the party freeze (47 of 84), the moment the nurse gave bad news (49 of 84) and 'I keep replaying the accident. It was my fault' (35 of 84). 'The price of taking part, worth paying' implies blame or is absurdly glib there.

line_before: They might have been jumping in with enthusiasm, not trying to shut you down.
line_now: They might have been jumping in with enthusiasm, not trying to shut you down.
why: Rare (4 of 84) even for 'He puts me down in front of people', where 311 ('a real pattern... worth addressing') is the top pick. A useful benign angle for ordinary interrupting.

line_before: Thoughts that arrive fast and loud often come from tiredness, stress or old experiences as much as from the facts in front of you.
line_now: Thoughts that arrive fast and loud often come from tiredness, stress or old experiences as much as from the facts in front of you.
why: A general angle (lowest weight), mostly seen once other lines have been used. It is hedged ('as much as') and non-clinical. Mild.

line_before: There might be a more ordinary explanation that hasn’t had a chance to come up yet.
why: A general angle offered for any heavy feeling, so its worst context is anything: bad results, dementia, abuse. A 'more ordinary explanation' for those is dismissive. Line 319 covers 'not enough information' safely.

line_before: They might be thinking about something that has nothing to do with you.
line_now: They might be thinking about something that has nothing to do with you.
why: It mismatches 'My dad hates me. He tells me every day that I ruined his life' (9 of 84), but it neither recasts the abuse as love nor blames the writer, unlike 261. It is a useful mind-reading line for ordinary worries.

line_before: What would you do if it went better than you expect?
why: future-reading kit, fired by 'never/never going to'. 70 of 84 for 'I am always in pain and it is never going to get better' (no label), and the top line (25 of 84) for 'We lost him last month. I will never hear his laugh again.' Cheery optimism there can land as cruel.

line_before: Try swapping the label for what actually happened: “I did this” instead of “I am this”.
line_now: Try swapping the label for what actually happened: “I did this” instead of “I am this”.
why: Confusing when the person labels someone else, but not harmful, and helpful for self-labels. Merely imperfect.

line_before: Most things land somewhere between perfect and disaster. Where on that line is this, really?
why: all-or-nothing kit. The top line for 'I am such a waste of space' (37 of 84 with sadness, 34 of 84 with no label), which passes the screen. The challenging 'really?' quizzes a self-hatred statement that often signals real distress.

line_before: What would a “partly good, partly not” version of this look like?
why: all-or-nothing kit. 27 of 84 for 'I am such a waste of space' (no label). Asking for a 'partly good' version of self-hatred, or of losing a home, reads as a worksheet.

line_before: Words like “always” and “never” are powerful, but they’re rarely exactly true.
why: always-never kit, fired by common words. 5 to 9 of 84 for 'I will never hear his laugh again' (literally true after a death), constant pain, 'Nobody cares whether I am here' and 'I just want everything to stop'. Correcting the person's wording lectures them when the 'never' may be true.

line_before: Can you think of even one exception? One is enough to loosen an “always”.
why: always-never kit. 14 to 17 of 84 for 'My dad calls me useless and stupid every day', and 9 of 84 for 'He always hurts me when he drinks'. Asking someone to find exceptions to abuse feeds 'he's not always like that'.

line_before: Lots of things shape how a situation goes. You might be one part of it, not the whole cause.
why: spotlight-on-me kit. The top line (30 of 84) for 'It is all my fault he gets so angry. I always set him off', which is victim-blaming, and 23 of 84 for 'It's my fault my parents split up', which confirms a child's partial blame. It contradicts the app's own abuse copy ('It's not your fault').

line_before: If the worst did happen, what would you do first? Having a plan can make it less scary.
why: worst-case-jump kit. 25 of 84 for 'Everything is falling apart and I can't cope' (no label). Asking someone who can't cope to picture 'the worst' and make 'a plan' is a risky pairing for undetected ideation, where 'plan' is a loaded word.

line_before: “Should” can turn a hope into a rule you’re failing. What happens if you swap it for “I’d like to”?
line_now: “Should” can turn a hope into a rule you’re failing. What happens if you swap it for “I’d like to”?
why: For 'I should see someone about how low I have been' (its top context, 25 of 84) the swap keeps the help-seeking intention ('I'd like to see someone'), so it doesn't undercut it. The grief wording is a little awkward but loosens a self-imposed timeline. Unlike 332, it keeps the intention.

line_before: Lots of “shoulds” come from other people’s timelines, not yours.
why: should-rules kit. 22 of 84 for 'I know I should see someone about how low I have been feeling but I keep putting it off', where it treats the urge to get help as someone else's rule, and it can weaken 'I should leave him'. It is lovely for grief timelines, but discouraging help-seeking for low mood is the worse risk.

line_before: The bad bit is real. It’s also not the only bit.
line_now: The bad bit is real. It’s also not the only bit.
why: It validates first ('is real') and doesn't question or blame. For intrusive trauma memories (13 to 16 of 84 for 'what he did to me') it is limited, not harmful. The real gap is the screen and routing for 'what he did to me'.

line_before: What else happened that you might be leaving out?
why: only-the-bad-bit kit. 17 of 84 for 'I can't stop thinking about what he did to me' (no label), which passes the screen. 'That you might be leaving out' sounds like disbelief or interrogation of a possible assault survivor.

line_before: The feeling is real and worth listening to. It just isn’t the same thing as proof.
why: feelings-as-proof kit. 10 of 84 for 'he is going to snap again and hurt the kids', where it undermines a gut sense of danger. 5 of 84 for 'I feel like everyone would be happier without me around', where 'worth listening to' lands on a known suicide warning belief.

line_before: A feeling can be strong even while the facts are still unclear.
why: feelings-as-proof kit. The top line (26 of 84) for 'My gut is telling me something is wrong with the baby, she has not moved much today', where reduced fetal movement needs checking straight away, and 23 of 84 for the fear he will hurt the kids. It implies an urgent warning can wait.

line_before: “What if” questions can go on forever. Try answering one: “Then I would…”
why: what-if-loop kit. 22 of 84 for 'What if I just was not here anymore? Would anyone even notice?' (loneliness), which passes the screen. It invites the person to complete a passive-ideation thought, with no pointer to help.

line_before: Your brain is trying to keep you safe. You can thank it, and still not follow every what-if.
why: what-if-loop kit. The top line (36 of 84) for the same 'What if I just was not here anymore?' text. It reads a passive wish not to be here as protective worry and offers no help. For 'what if he hurts me' it tells the person not to follow a real threat.

line_now: Oh, that sounds really hard. We can take this one slowly, together.
why: Found by the Tier 0 code review. Harm at home now gets only tender openers, and Pipzi had one ('Oh. That’s a big feeling. Let’s be soft with it.'), so it opened every account of abuse Pipzi answered. A second tender opener in Pipzi's warm, together voice, without the curiosity that asks the person to look at it again. Tender, not soft: it assumes the feeling is hard.

line_now: Let’s find a sheltered spot under a big old tree, and take this slowly.
why: Found by the Tier 0 code review. Zuzu's only tender opener was line 30 ('the big, wide sky that can hold it'), so ongoing abuse, now always given a tender opener, got 'hold it' imagery every time. A second one in Zuzu's outdoor imagination: shelter and going slowly, asking the person to hold nothing. Soft: it doesn't assume the feeling is hard, so grief told with a happy label can have it too.
